cands.name: Lakesha Womack

money.note: Individuals gave $53,779; PAC money $1,000; candidate's own money $3,205. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Democratic nominee for North Carolina's 14th Congressional District. Business consultant and ordained minister. Founder of Womack Consulting Group and Chief Strategy Officer at ASPIRE Community Capital, a community development lender. Vanderbilt graduate. Has not previously held elected office.

controversies.text: Deputies served Womack with a felony warrant on Oct. 11, 2026. The 2020 warrant charges her with failing to return a rental car, worth $20,000 by the warrant's value, rented in October 2019. She called it an ongoing legal matter, said her court date is after Election Day, and cited a past health issue and financial rebuilding.

cands.gaps: We could not find her birthplace or exact birth year; Wikipedia gives 1976 or 1977. She has held no elected office, so there is no voting record or record of official actions. We found no stated positions from her on data centers, development and growth, homestead property taxes, foreign or investor land buying, immigration or H-1B visas, policing, gun laws or school vouchers. Her education platform says she backs public school funding and fairly paid teachers, but it does not address vouchers or charters. We could not find court records or reporting that resolve the 2019 rental-vehicle matter. The only North Carolina residency date we found is her own statement of 2016, reported by Wikipedia. Her endorsements on Ballotpedia are online voter-guide groups, which we did not treat as notable endorsements.

cands.bio: Attorney and Republican politician from Kings Mountain. Served in the North Carolina House from 2003 to 2025, including as Speaker from 2015 to 2025. Has been U.S. representative for North Carolina's 14th District since January 2025. Earlier was Cleveland County GOP chair and a UNC Board of Governors member.

controversies.text: Federal records show $20,000 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $35,078 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26.
Missed 2 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (0.3%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 1, 2025-03-11 to 2025-03-11.

In 2016 a senior Moore aide asked state environmental staff about fuel tanks at a Siler City poultry plant Moore co-owned and was selling. The plant later got a $22,000 tank reimbursement. Moore said he knew nothing of the calls. DEQ staff said they felt no pressure. A 2018 complaint was dismissed; a second was filed in 2019.

In 2012 Moore's Kings Mountain law practice received a $62,000 state-approved development grant. NC Newsline reported this led to warnings that he should avoid conflicts of interest or the appearance of them. Moore's response was not found in the reporting.

In 2022 former state Rep. Holly Grange, a UNC-Wilmington trustee, said she was removed from the board because she refused to back Moore's preferred chancellor candidate. A House bill was filed to replace her before her term ended. Moore's response was not found in the reporting.

In June 2025 Moore reportedly did not disclose stock purchases made around the April 2025 tariff announcement, which Wikipedia describes as a STOCK Act disclosure violation. It also reports July 2025 purchases of Intel stock and of Centene and UnitedHealth stock, the latter sold at a profit in August. A spokesperson denied he took part in insider trading. The page cites no court or official finding.
In 2015 a local journalist's article prompted an FBI inquiry into Moore's campaign reports. The FBI declined to comment and no charges were ever filed.

cands.gaps: We could not find Tim Moore's own statements on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on out-of-state or foreign land buyers, growth and land conservation, immigration and H-1B, police pay, guns, abortion or school choice. We also found no documented stance on data centers or development. The source we could read covered only broad career and controversy summaries and did not name the specific bills he passed, so we left out deeds on most issues. His education and career history rest on a single encyclopedia-style page with no primary documents, and we found no endorsements.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.
